paper_title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A world model that renders the consequences of policys actions can serve as simulator: rollouts become parallel, repeatable, and free of the risk of damaging hardware. This sidesteps both the danger and the sample cost of online training on real hardware [43, 61, 64, 65], and avoids the sim-to-real gap [19, 34] and the per-environment engineering that hand-built physics simulators demand. The idea runs from model-based 1 Figure 1 PrimeSim. (a) The midtraining corpus: roughly 30.1K hours of curated robot data spanning humanoid, dual-arm, single-arm and handheld UMI [3, 14] platforms, mixing real and simulated footage. (b) The model is conditioned on language prompt, unified action representation over head, torso, waist, end-effector, gripper and chassis, and three camera views, and predicts future frames; post-training makes generation autoregressive with selected KV-cache memory at four denoising steps. (c) Capabilities: fidelity against prior systems, action following measured against simulation ground truth, few-shot adaptation to an unseen embodiment, and use as simulator: success rate in PrimeSim predicts success rate in the LIBERO [51] physics simulator with = 0.99, so policies can be trained in the model and the result carried back to the robot. reinforcement learning, where agents learn from imagined rollouts alone [3032, 79], through interactive video generation for games and open-ended worlds [4, 7, 20, 23, 55, 66, 73], to action-conditioned robot world models [25, 26, 29, 50]. What such model must do is narrower than generating plausible video: it must adhere to the actions policy issues, keep several camera views consistent, and stay coherent over rollouts far longer than the window it was trained on. We present PrimeSim, world model built as robot simulator that meets all three requirements. To enable faithful action following and consistent multiview generation, we adapt pretrained video model to robot dynamics through midtraining on 30,110 hours of demonstrations spanning 22 robot platforms. For action following, we unify heterogeneous robot controls into shared action representation and introduce frame-aligned dual-path action conditioning, combining temporally aligned attention with direct action injection to establish precise correspondence between robot controls and generated motion. For multiview consistency, we introduce view-aware interleaved attention, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving camera-specific representations through explicit camera identities. Through joint conditional flow-matching training, these designs allow single model to learn action-conditioned, multiview robot dynamics across diverse embodiments, establishing the foundation for an interactive world model simulator. While midtraining establishes action-conditioned multiview generation within fixed temporal window, turning the model into practical robot simulator introduces fundamental challenge: autoregressive simulation requires continuously conditioning on the models own imperfect predictions, whereas conventional video generators are trained on fixed-length, ground-truth contexts. This mismatch leads to error accumulation over extended rollouts and is compounded by the computational cost of iterative video generation. To address these challenges, we develop fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that progressively 2 transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient, long-horizon autoregressive simulator. First, we enable fast generation through chunk-causal adaptation and four-step consistency distillation, making sequential simulation and subsequent self-rollout training computationally tractable. Second, we improve self-conditioned stability through self-rollout training with asymmetric distribution matching against the frozen bidirectional teacher, allowing the model to learn from its own generated histories rather than relying solely on ground-truth context. Third, we introduce hierarchical temporal memory to support long-horizon coherence, preserving the initial scene, sparse long-term history, and dense recent motion within bounded KV cache. Together, these components enable efficient autoregressive simulation that remains robust to self-generated context and scales beyond the original training window. Together, these designs enable PrimeSim to generate temporally coherent rollouts up to 105 seconds at 10.1 FPS, supporting diverse robotic manipulation tasks involving both rigid and deformable objects. Compared with five open-source action-conditioned world models, PrimeSim achieves state-of-the-art performance on WorldSimProbe [16], leading four of its five suites: global trajectory coverage by 10.0%, action-source behavior preservation by 41.8%, and interaction dynamics by 48.4%, each measured against the strongest competing model on that axis, with interaction grounding also led at 85.7. On EWMBench, PrimeSim reaches the best overall score of 6.09, ahead of both GE-Sim variants (5.82 and 5.79) and every instruction-conditioned model, and is best on five of the eight dimensions, including perfect scores on high-level semantics, trajectory alignment and logical consistency, with action semantics (BLEU) 72.7% above the strongest GE-Sim variant. Beyond benchmark fidelity, we demonstrate the practical utility of PrimeSim as learned simulator for GRPO-based policy optimization [27], enabling policy improvement through model-generated interactions. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code to support further research. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that transforms pretrained video generator into an interactive robot world model through progressive midtraining and posttraining framework. We develop large-scale midtraining framework using 30,110 hours of demonstrations across 22 robot platforms. With unified cross-embodiment action representations, frame-aligned dual-path conditioning, and view-aware interleaved attention, PrimeSim learns action-faithful and multiviewconsistent robot dynamics across diverse embodiments. We introduce fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that combines efficient causal generation, self-rollout training with asymmetric distribution matching, and hierarchical temporal memory. This enables fast, self-conditioned autoregressive simulation while mitigating long-horizon error accumulation beyond the original training window. We demonstrate strong performance across diverse rigid and deformable object manipulation tasks: 10.1 FPS at four sampling steps, coherent rollouts of up to 105 seconds, 6.09 overall on EWMBench (first), and first on four of five WorldSimProbe suites against five open-source action-conditioned world models, retaining the lead on two of the three action-realisation axes and interaction dynamics. We further validate PrimeSim as learned simulator for GRPO-based policy optimization.

sections.title: 2 Data Engine
sections.content: Our goal for training data was to learn from massive and diverse pool of settings while keeping our representations simple. To this end, we assembled 30,110 hours of robot demonstration data from mix of open-source and proprietary sources. Dataset statistics are shown in Fig. 3, and an overview of the datasets used is provided in Table 12. In general, we include any demonstration data that can be converted into our unified format with reasonable effort, whether humanoid, dual-arm, single-arm, UMI [14], or simulated. We describe the conversion pipeline, quality filtering, and dataset composition below and in the appendix. Robot Data Pooling. Motivated by the low cost of data collection, recent state-of-the-art methods pretrain on large egocentric human videos with smaller ratio of robot data [25, 45, 83]. However, aligning robot actions to latent actions or predicted hand-to-end-effector poses adds additional complexity. Since pooled 3 Figure 2 Overview of the data pipeline. Raw demonstrations from teleoperation, UMI, and simulation are converted through four stages: video quality filtering, action quality filtering, action preprocessing, and data alignment. Each stage lists the operations applied to the incoming data. The pipeline produces unified corpus of 30,110 hours across 20 dataset families and 22 robot platforms  (Table 12)  . robot datasets, openand closed-source together, now largely match the scale of the egocentric corpora those models relied on, we skip the alignment problem entirely: we train directly on robot demonstrations from both sources and simply unify their action and state spaces using the general action representation described in Sec. 3.2.1. Dataset Staging. Each training stage serves different purpose, so each should be trained on different data distribution. For midtraining, we require vast and highly diverse data sources, so we use the entire dataset. For posttraining, the model has already seen the full corpus and the stage mainly aims to improve long-horizon and real-time responsiveness rather than to broaden coverage. We therefore train it on small datasets collected for specific downstream tasks, which are long enough to contain complete episodes and representative of what the deployed simulator is asked to continue, rather than on subsample of the pretraining mixture.

Datasets with dexterous hands or humanoid legs represent small fraction of the pooled corpus. To keep the action representation simple, we filter these datasets out. We discard sequences whose action signals contain discontinuities inconsistent with continuous robot motion. We detect these as outliers in the first difference of each action channel: an isolated step change far outside the distribution of adjacent steps indicates sensor or logging fault rather than commanded acceleration. Datasets containing corrupted video frames, or action values outside their admissible range, are discarded as well. Missing action detection. Some datasets leave certain action features blank, such as end-effector pose or chassis velocity. If these values cannot be recovered through forward kinematics, the affected data is dropped. 2.1.3 Stage 3: Data Alignment Frequency alignment. We preserve each datasets native sampling rate at collection time, but resample to fixed 10 Hz during training. If dataset cannot be resampled to exactly 10 Hz within 0.03 timestamp tolerance, we use the closest achievable frequency. Camera alignment. The number of cameras varies across embodiments. To make batches collatable, we fix the models camera count to three. Datasets with more than three cameras have their uncommon cameras dropped; datasets with fewer have the primary camera repeated until three slots are filled. Prompt alignment. Datasets differ in whether they provide natural-language task descriptions. For datasets that include prompts, we keep them as is. For datasets that do not, we generate prompt from the task metadata with template-based generator, so that every training sample is paired with task description. Format conversion. sections.title: 3 PrimeSim
sections.content: PrimeSim aims to serve as world model simulator for long-horizon robot manipulation, generating future camera observations conditioned on robot actions. Unlike conventional video generation, robot simulation requires the model to faithfully execute prescribed actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and preserve coherent scene dynamics over extended trajectories. Moreover, the simulator must support low-latency autoregressive generation to enable efficient interaction with robot policies. 6 To address these requirements, we adopt progressive training framework that transforms pretrained video generator into an action-conditioned, multiview, autoregressive simulator. We first initialize PrimeSim from pretrained video generation backbone that provides general visual and motion priors. During midtraining, we introduce structured action conditioning and multiview adaptation to learn robot dynamics from largescale demonstrations. During posttraining, we progressively adapt the model for causal generation, few-step sampling, and long-horizon self-conditioned rollouts with persistent temporal memory.

sections.title: 3.1 Pretrain
sections.content: We initialize from the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B pretrained weights [75], which provides strong generative prior over natural video: object permanence, lighting and material statistics, and short-horizon motion patterns that would be prohibitively expensive to relearn from robot data alone. This stage establishes the general world priors, spatiotemporal coherence and high-fidelity texture that the later stages build on. We adopt this checkpoint as given: all of our own training happens in the midtraining and posttraining stages that follow.

sections.title: 3.2 Midtrain
sections.content: Midtraining adapts the pretrained video generator to action-conditioned robot dynamics. While the pretrained backbone provides general visual and motion priors, it lacks explicit control over robot actions and consistent generation across multiple camera views. To address these limitations, we introduce three complementary components: unified cross-embodiment action representation, frame-aligned dual-path conditioning, and view-aware interleaved attention. We jointly train these components with the video generation backbone on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms (Sec. 2). Problem Formulation. Our objective during midtraining is to learn the visual consequences of prescribed robot actions across multiple camera views. At robot timestep t, let ot = (It, qt) denote the observation, where It = (I1 Given an observation context Ot = (otK+1, . . . , ot), an H-step action trajectory At = (at+1, . . . , at+H), and an optional language instruction ℓ, we formulate multiview video prediction as ) contains images from cameras and qt represents the robots proprioceptive state. , . . . , In It+1:t+H WBD( Ot, At, ℓ), (5) where WBD denotes the bidirectional world model learned during midtraining. Unlike autoregressive simulation, the model jointly predicts the future video within fixed temporal window. This formulation provides the foundation for the action and multiview conditioning mechanisms described below. 3.2.1 Action Representation We define actions as changes in robot poses. Given consecutive video tokens, an action token at denotes the pose change that produces the transition into latent frame t. Each embodiment source is transformed into fixed 31-dimensional representation that captures shared underlying geometric structure across different action domains, with the slots an embodiment lacks set to zero. General Action Representation. At high level, actions can include up to four components: effector poses for the agents effectors, grasp states, pose of the head, waist, and torso, and the chassis velocity. To cover manipulation poses across almost all robot platforms pose representation, we represent arm states as end-effector poses, grasp states as binary flags, head/torso/waist as joint angles, and the chassis as planar velocity (vx, vy, ω). As each embodiments degrees of freedom varies, we leave redundancy in each joint slot to account for this (see Fig. 5). 7 Figure 5 General action representation in PrimeSim, covering single-arm, bimanual, UMI, and wheeled humanoid embodiments. Relative Action Chunk. All actions are defined relative to the initial frame of each window, i.e., at+it = at+i at. This relative action representation for conditioning resolves several core issues in cross-embodiment learning. First, embodiments with missing features can simply be represented as 0 (no movement). Second, the absolute origin offset of each embodiment is cancelled out by the relative transformation. Third, it strengthens the per-frame action conditioning signal by grounding all changes to the conditioning first frame, as well as concentrating the action distribution. Relative actions have been explored in prior models, but with deltas taken from the previous frame [25]. We argue that anchoring to the first conditional frame of the window instead provides stronger conditioning signal for world models. An ablation for relative action chunk is provided in Table 9. 3.2.2 Action Conditioning Effectively controlling world model to generate future frames that faithfully follow commanded actions remains fundamental challenge. Existing models often hallucinate robot motions inconsistent with the conditioned actions [13, 67]. We attribute this limitation in part to the lack of explicit temporal alignment between actions and generated frames. Under standard global attention, each frame can aggregate action information from multiple timesteps, making it difficult to identify which action should govern its evolution. To address this, we introduce frame-aligned dual-path conditioning mechanism, which strengthens actionframe correspondence by explicitly binding actions to their corresponding frames through two complementary pathways. while the second directly injects action information into frame representations, ensuring that action conditioning does not rely solely on attention routing. Together with our first-frame-anchored relative action representation, these designs provide temporally precise and explicit control over generated robot motions. We evaluate their individual contributions in Table 10. Action Tokenizer. To enable frame-aligned conditioning, we first establish temporal correspondence between robot actions and video latents. Specifically, we encode each relative action chunk into compact sequence of latent action tokens using two-layer MLP, producing one action token for each latent video frame. This representation provides shared temporal structure for the two conditioning pathways described below, allowing each frame to be associated with the action responsible for its evolution. Framewise Action-Conditioning. Given the aligned action tokens, our first conditioning pathway explicitly constrains how actions interact with video representations. Rather than allowing every frame to attend to actions from arbitrary timesteps, we introduce shifted-diagonal attention mask that restricts frame-to-action attention to the corresponding temporal transition. Specifically, since action at drives the transition into frame + 1, frame attends only to at1, while the initial conditioning frame receives no action conditioning. This prevents interference from temporally unrelated actions and establishes an explicit actionframe correspondence at the attention level. While prior work has explored frame-level action conditioning [29], our approach enforces this correspondence directly through the attention mask and combines it with first-frame-anchored relative action chunks, which specify the intended motion relative to consistent reference state. Action-Frame Adapter. Although framewise attention establishes which action each frame should attend to, it does not guarantee that the corresponding action signal sufficiently influences the frame representation. In particular, action information may still be underweighted when competing with rich visual features during attention. We therefore introduce complementary conditioning pathway that directly injects the aligned action information into each frame token. Specifically, lightweight actionframe adapter computes residual feature shift from the corresponding action token and integrates it into the frame representation (Figure 4). Unlike attention-based conditioning, this pathway provides direct route for action information, independent of the learned attention weights. The two pathways thus serve distinct but complementary roles: framewise attention determines which action governs each frame, while the adapter ensures that the selected action directly modulates its representation. Their combination strengthens actionframe binding and encourages generated motions to remain consistent with the specified action trajectory. 8 3.2.3 Multiview Adaption fundamental challenge in action-conditioned multiview generation is ensuring that different camera views remain consistent with the same evolving physical scene. This is particularly challenging in robotics, where wrist-mounted cameras move with the robot and may observe one another, creating strong dependencies across views. Treating each view independently can lead to inconsistent robot motions and object interactions, while unrestricted global attention may obscure view-specific information. To address this, we introduce view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, which enables cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. Specifically, we organize the 30 DiT blocks to alternate between intra-view and global attention: two out of every three blocks restrict attention to tokens within each camera view, while every third block enables information exchange across all three views. This design allows the model to capture view-specific spatial and temporal relationships locally, while periodically integrating information across cameras to maintain coherent representation of the shared physical scene. However, effective cross-view interaction also requires the model to distinguish the source of each visual token, particularly when features from different cameras are mixed through global attention. We therefore prepend dedicated camera token to each view, explicitly encoding its view identity throughout the generation process. The two designs serve complementary roles: interleaved attention controls how information is exchanged across views, while camera tokens preserve which view each representation belongs to. Together, they promote consistent multiview generation without sacrificing view-specific information (Figure 4). We validate the contribution of both components in Table 11. 3.2.4 Training Objective Having established the unified action representation, frame-aligned action conditioning, and view-aware multiview attention, we jointly optimize these components under conditional latent flow-matching objective. Rather than introducing separate objectives for action following or multiview consistency, both capabilities are learned through the conditional generation of future multiview observations. Importantly, all camera views are generated jointly, and robot actions are incorporated directly into the velocity prediction network through the proposed conditioning mechanisms. This allows the model to learn action-conditioned visual dynamics and cross-view dependencies under unified generative objective. The resulting bidirectional world model WBD provides the foundation for subsequent autoregressive adaptation. During posttraining, we retain flow matching for initial causal adaptation, while introducing consistency distillation and distribution matching to enable efficient, self-conditioned, long-horizon simulation. 9 Figure 6 Overview of the post-training pipeline, from the midtrained base model through the four adaptation stages to the deployed simulator.

sections.title: 3.3 Posttrain
sections.content: Midtraining equips PrimeSim with the ability to predict action-conditioned, multiview robot videos within fixed temporal window. However, accurate short-horizon generation does not by itself yield practical world model simulator. The midtrained model generates clips with bidirectional attention and requires many denoising steps, whereas policy interaction calls for continuously extending rollout from the models own predictions. This introduces three additional challenges: autoregressive generation must respect temporal causality, sampling must be fast enough for repeated rollouts, and errors and missing scene context must not accumulate uncontrollably over long horizons. We therefore posttrain PrimeSim to transform fixed-window video prediction into fast, self-conditioned, long-horizon simulation. Our guiding principle is fast video, slow memory: generate each new chunk with few-step sampling while retaining informative history across much longer timescales. We realize this through four progressive stages: (1) causal adaptation enables chunk-wise autoregressive generation; (2) consistency distillation produces four-step sampler; (3) clip-level self-rollout with asymmetric distribution matching improves generation conditioned on the models own outputs; and (4) episode-level adaptation combines self-rollout training with bounded, multiscale temporal memory. The stages are sequential: causal generation enables rollout, fast sampling makes rollout training tractable, and self-conditioned training prepares the model for long-horizon continuation. 3.3.1 Stage 1: Autoregressive Modelling To enable continuous simulation, we first adapt the bidirectional model WBD obtained from midtraining into chunk-causal model WC. Unlike the midtrained model, which jointly generates all frames within fixed temporal window, the causal model generates video chunks sequentially, conditioned on previously generated observations. We achieve this through chunk-causal attention, which preserves bidirectional attention within each chunk while restricting cross-chunk attention to preceding chunks. This allows the model to retain its learned action-conditioned multiview generation capabilities while supporting autoregressive prediction. Specifically, we adopt teacher forcing [9, 18, 36, 85, 101] during causal adaptation, where each chunk is conditioned on clean ground-truth history. Let Bi,clean and Bi,noisy denote the clean and noisy representations of chunk i, respectively. The attention context for each noisy chunk is defined as (cid:0)Bi,noisy (cid:1) = (cid:110) Bj,clean : < (cid:111) (cid:8)Bi,noisy (cid:9) , (8) where S() denotes the accessible attention context. This design prevents information leakage from future chunks while allowing all chunks to be trained in parallel. The same chunk partition also determines the noise granularity of the diffusion-forcing objective. Stage 1 therefore keeps the flow-matching loss of Eq. 7; what changes is the attention mask the loss is evaluated under, which is what we mean by diffusion forcing rather than new objective. Through this adaptation, PrimeSim acquires the ability to generate future observations autoregressively 10 rather than within fixed bidirectional window. However, teacher forcing introduces an exposure bias: the model is trained with clean historical observations but must condition on its own imperfect predictions at inference. Increasing the chunk size from = 1 to = 3 reduces the number of sequential generation chunks from nine to three in our training window, mitigating but not eliminating error accumulation. To enable subsequent training on self-generated histories, we first reduce the computational cost of autoregressive generation through few-step distillation in Stage 2. 3.3.2 Stage 2: Causal Consistency Distillation Although Stage 1 enables autoregressive generation, the resulting causal model WC still requires 50 denoising steps per chunk, making continuous simulation computationally expensive. More importantly, the high sampling cost makes it impractical to train on self-generated rollouts, where gradients must propagate through multiple generation chunks. To address this, we adopt Causal Consistency Distillation (Causal CD) [97] to obtain an efficient four-step generator. Specifically, we use WC as frozen causal teacher and initialize causal student Wθ from its weights. Both models share the same chunk-causal architecture, allowing the student to preserve the autoregressive structure learned in Stage 1 while substantially reducing the number of sampling steps. Rather than supervising the student with complete teacher-generated trajectories, Causal CD performs online distillation by matching local transitions of the teachers flow trajectory. Let xt denote noisy video latent at flow time t, ˆx0,C the teachers clean estimate, and xC tt the target obtained from local teacher ODE step. The distillation objective is LCD(θ) = xt,t,t (cid:104) w(t) (cid:16) Gθ(xt, ˆx0,C, t), xC tt (cid:17)(cid:105) , (9) where Gθ denotes the students local flow-map update and d(, ) measures the discrepancy between student and teacher transitions. By matching nearby flow states, the student learns to approximate the teachers multi-step generation process with substantially fewer sampling steps. Moreover, the online objective requires only local teacher ODE step per update, avoiding the expensive precomputation and storage of complete teacher trajectories. To further reduce the memory overhead of maintaining teacher and student models simultaneously, we optimize LoRA [33] adapters while keeping the midtrained backbone weights frozen. Together, these designs produce four-step causal student that substantially accelerates autoregressive generation and, crucially, makes self-rollout training computationally tractable. Nevertheless, distillation alone does not resolve the exposure bias inherited from teacher-forced training, nor does it guarantee visual fidelity under repeated self-conditioned generation. We therefore further optimize the distilled student on its own generated rollouts in Stage 3.

sections.title: 3.3.3 Stage 3: Clip-Level Self-Rollout with Asymmetric DMD
sections.content: Although Stage 2 substantially accelerates autoregressive generation, the distilled student Wθ still faces two limitations. First, training with clean historical observations introduces exposure bias, as the model must condition on its own imperfect predictions during inference. Second, consistency distillation has forward-KL-like, mode-covering effect, potentially producing averaged predictions with reduced perceptual detail. To address both limitations, we introduce clip-level self-rollout training with asymmetric distribution matching. Specifically, the student autoregressively generates video chunks within each training clip, with subsequent chunks conditioned on its own previously generated latents through the causal KV cache, rather than on ground-truth history. This exposes the model to the conditioning distribution encountered during inference. To preserve generation quality under self-conditioned rollouts, we further optimize the student using an asymmetric Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) objective [89, 90]. Unlike Stage 2, which distills causal teacher into causal student, we now use the frozen bidirectional model WBD from midtraining as the reference teacher. This design exploits the stronger fixed-window generation capability of the bidirectional 11 model to supervise the autoregressive student, without imposing the teachers bidirectional attention structure on the student. We adopt the mode-seeking reverse-KL objective DKL (pθ( c) pBD( c)) , (10) where pθ and pBD denote the conditional distributions of the causal student and bidirectional reference model, respectively, and represents the corresponding conditioning information, including visual context, robot actions, and camera-view identities. To optimize this objective, we introduce trainable fake-score network vϕ that estimates the distribution of student-generated samples. Together with the frozen bidirectional reference, it provides the score difference used to update the student. Let x0 denote the clean video latent generated by the student, and let ˆx0,ϕ and ˆx0,BD denote the clean-sample estimates of the fake-score network and bidirectional teacher, respectively, evaluated on the same noisy latent. We construct the normalized score-difference direction as KL = ˆx0,ϕ ˆx0,BD max(E x0 ˆx0,BD , δ) , δ = 108, (11) where the normalization stabilizes the update when the students generated distribution deviates substantially from the reference. The student is optimized using the surrogate loss Lgen(θ) = 1 2 x0 sg ( x0 KL)2 2 , (12) where sg denotes the stop-gradient operator. Meanwhile, the fake-score network is trained on studentgenerated samples using the standard flow matching objective, Lcritic(ϕ) = x0,ϵ,τ (cid:104)(cid:13) (cid:13)vϕ(xτ, τ, c) (ϵ x0)(cid:13) (cid:13) (cid:105) 2 2 , (13) where xτ = (1 τ) x0 + τϵ is the noisy interpolation of the generated latent, and ϵ (0, I). Through clip-level self-rollout and asymmetric distribution matching, Stage 3 enables the four-step causal student to learn from its own generated history while receiving high-quality supervision from the bidirectional reference. However, training remains confined to fixed-length clips, whereas practical robot simulation requires coherent generation over complete episodes. This remaining short-traininglong-inference gap motivates the episode-level self-rollout and persistent temporal memory introduced in Stage 4. 3.3.4 Stage 4: Episode-Level Long-Horizon Adaptation While Stage 3 enables self-conditioned generation within short clips, reliable robot simulation requires maintaining coherent predictions over trajectories far longer than the training window. At this scale, two challenges become particularly critical: prediction errors accumulate as generated chunks repeatedly serve as future conditioning, and important scene information may be lost from recent context due to occlusion or camera motion. To address both challenges, we extend self-rollout training from fixed-length clips to complete robot episodes and introduce persistent hierarchical temporal memory. The former exposes the model to long-horizon error accumulation during training, while the latter preserves scene information across multiple temporal scales. Together, they enable the student to generate extended trajectories using its own predictions rather than relying on clean historical observations. Stage 4 inherits the asymmetric DMD objective of Stage 3 unchanged. What changes is what the rollouts span: the student is now supervised on episodes rather than fixed clips, so the distribution it is matched against includes the errors it accumulates over long horizon rather than only over few chunks. Episode-level self-rollout. We first extend self-conditioned generation to complete robot episodes, allowing the student to experience the long-horizon conditioning distribution encountered during inference. Specifically, the student generates successive video chunks autoregressively, with each continuation conditioned on its own previously generated history through the causal KV cache. Generator gradients are accumulated 12 across the episode, followed by single optimization update at the episode boundary. Meanwhile, the fake-score network is updated after each generated window to track the evolving student distribution. The KV cache persists throughout the episode and is reset only when new episode begins. Unlike clip-level training, this procedure directly exposes the student to errors that accumulate across successive generations, encouraging more stable long-horizon predictions. Memory in world models is usually conditioned on encoded ground-truth observations [29, 50, 63, 67] or on cache of clean historical frames [81, 86, 92]. Both supply, at inference, data the model does not itself produce, which opens train-inference gap. PrimeSim instead trains its memory on its own rollouts, so the distribution it conditions on during training is the one it will have at inference. Hierarchical temporal memory. Although episode-level self-rollout exposes the model to longer trajectories, it does not by itself prevent the loss of historical information. Retaining every generated frame is computationally expensive, while keeping only recent frames can discard important scene states. We therefore introduce hierarchical temporal memory that organizes the KV cache into three complementary components: global sink, slow memory, and local memory. The global sink retains the initial observed latent state as persistent reference throughout the episode. The local memory stores recent consecutive generated latents, preserving fine-grained motion information. The slow memory, in contrast, maintains sparsely sampled representation of longer-term history. After each generation window, the previous local-memory entries are merged with the existing slow-memory bank and temporally downsampled to fixed capacity, while the newly generated latents populate the next local-memory bank. Temporal positions are preserved during downsampling, and synchronized frame indices are used across all camera views to maintain aligned multiview histories. This hierarchical design allows each generated chunk to access the initial scene, sparse long-term context, and dense recent motion within bounded memory budget. Importantly, except for the initial observed state, all memory entries originate from the students own generated history. The same memory update mechanism is used during training and inference, avoiding the distribution mismatch introduced by teacher-forced historical context. Latent-space continuation. To further improve the efficiency and consistency of long-horizon generation, we maintain the students continuation entirely in latent space. Rather than decoding each generated segment and re-encoding it as new conditioning observation, the student carries its history forward through the persistent KV cache. Continuation windows receive neither new first-frame latent nor clean ground-truth prefix, ensuring that the autoregressive process remains conditioned on the models own predictions. This avoids repeated video decoding and encoding along the generation path and allows the student to extend trajectories without repeatedly reinitializing visual context. Amortized supervision. remaining challenge is supervising episode-length student rollouts using the bidirectional reference and fake-score networks, which operate within fixed temporal windows. We decouple long-horizon generation from local distribution supervision. For each continuation, we decode the preceding segment once and re-encode only its final frame as conditioning observation for the score networks, as required by the causal VAE. This operation is performed outside the students gradient path, and the re-encoded observation is never fed back into the students autoregressive generation. Consequently, the student can accumulate history across complete episodes, while the score networks evaluate local transitions within their original temporal windows. This enables long-horizon self-rollout training without extending the temporal context of the supervising models. Action re-anchoring. Finally, to preserve consistent action conditioning across long rollouts, we express actions relative to the reference pose recorded at the beginning of each episode, rather than resetting the reference at every generation window. This maintains consistent action coordinate frame across continuation boundaries and prevents changes in the reference frame from introducing ambiguity into the conditioned motion trajectory. Together, the four posttraining stages transform PrimeSim from fixed-window, action-conditioned video generator into fast, self-conditioned, long-horizon world model simulator. Few-step distillation enables efficient autoregressive generation, while episode-level self-rollout and hierarchical temporal memory support coherent simulation across extended robot trajectories. At inference, PrimeSim requires only the four-step causal student and its bounded KV cache, generating future multiview observations conditioned on robot actions without access to ground-truth future frames.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: Six sets of experiments follow, in the order the papers argument develops. We first place PrimeSim against existing world models on benchmarks built for embodied prediction, together with the inference cost that decides whether model can serve as simulator at all. We then ask what midtraining actually acquires, by adapting to platforms and to scenes and camera placements the model has never seen. We examine what post-training changes over long horizons, whether the simulator is faithful enough to evaluate and to improve policy, and finally which of the design choices carry the result.

sections.title: 4.1 Comparison to the State of the Art
sections.content: We compare on three axes, chosen because simulator has to be right about different things than video generator. Trajectory fidelity asks whether the commanded motion is actually realised; scene and semantic consistency asks whether the world still looks and means the same while that motion happens; and inference cost asks whether the model can be run inside control loop at all. WorldSimProbe separates the first two into its own axes, EWMBench aggregates them into single score, and neither measures the third, so we report throughput separately. 4.1.1 WorldSimProbe Evaluation WorldSimProbe [16] isolates property that reconstruction metrics do not capture: whether world model behaves as simulator. It is built on the Observable Simulator Contract, which requires that supplied actions induce corresponding agent motion, and that the environment respond to that realized motion rather than to the action that was merely commanded. This targets failure mode invisible to PSNR, in which the robot does not move as instructed while the scene reacts as though it had. The benchmark decomposes the observable simulator contract into five diagnostic suites. T1 (Local Action Calibration) tests whether the model reproduces the simulators response to small and large action perturbations. T2 (Global Trajectory Coverage) evaluates whether it follows globally different but physically executable trajectories transferred across tasks and scenes. T3 (Action-Source Behavior Preservation) examines whether behavioral differences among expert, human-teleoperated, and policy-generated actions, such as speed, smoothness, and corrective motion, are retained. T4 (Interaction Grounding) uses validated no-contact counterfactuals to test whether the model avoids hallucinating interactions unsupported by the realized robot motion. T5 (Interaction Dynamics) assesses whether both robot motion and object response match intended interaction primitives such as pushing, pulling, rotating, shaking, and dropping. We evaluate PrimeSim with sink token that provides lightweight historical context for bidirectional architectures. To improve physical understanding, we additionally construct training data from three sources: multiple trajectories sampled from VLA task executions, perturbed variants of these sampled trajectories, and trajectories obtained after randomly replacing objects in the scene. Random visual noise is also applied during training to reduce the distribution shift caused by the mismatch between training and evaluation resolutions. PrimeSim generates 192 256 images per view and predicts 33 frames at 10 FPS. Because the benchmark does not explicitly score appearance, task success, or coarse rollout-level responsiveness, the resulting comparison is primarily behavioral, and high scores indicate simulator fidelity rather than visual quality or downstream utility. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models, PrimeSim ranks first on four of the five suites, leading two of the three action realization axes (T2 at 67.9 and T3 at 72.3) and interaction dynamics (T5 at 37.1). The one axis we do not win is informative rather than incidental. LingBot-VA leads local action calibration (77.0 against 70.2), indicating that our fine-grained control precision is not yet the best in the field even where coarse trajectory coverage is. sections.title: 4.2 What Midtraining Learns
sections.content: Midtraining is where the model acquires its action interface: action conditioning and multiview coupling are introduced and trained over 20 dataset families and 22 robot platforms (Sec. 3.2). The question we ask here is what else that stage leaves behind. If cross-embodiment training yields transferable features rather than fit to the training distribution, those features should survive transfer along three axes at once: to platforms the model has never driven, to scenes it has never seen, and to camera placements it has never been mounted at. All three survive, and the first does so at cost low enough to change what adding new robot means in practice: an action-following rollout within 100 to 200 gradient steps, where the pretrained backbone does not reach one at ten to twenty times the budget. At learning rate of 3 105, two hundred steps move the parameters by roughly 102, so this is small amount of optimisation rather than finetune to convergence. The comparison therefore tests what midtraining already provides, not how much can be recovered by fitting each new platform. The protocol is in Table 4. Posttraining is analysed separately in Sec. 4.3, because it changes how the model is run rather than what it has learned. Table 4 Few-shot adaptation to held-out embodiments. Both initialisations are finetuned under an identical recipe with single-trajectory batches at batch size of 1 and learning rate of 3 105, and neither receives an embodiment identifier or any embodiment-specific parameters. Entries are gradient steps to an action-following rollout, meaning one in which the arm tracks the commanded trajectory and the scene responds to the motion actually realized. No action-following rollout was reached within this budget. Midtraining and posttraining are designed to broaden the models coverage of embodiments and dynamics. We probe whether that coverage has in fact yielded transferable knowledge by asking what new platform costs. We hold out three platforms from the 20 dataset families of our training corpus  (Table 12)  : single 7-DoF arm (xArm 7) drawn from Open X-Embodiment [17], bimanual platform (ViperX 300, as used by ALOHA [98]) and the original Stanford UMI gripper [14]. Similar embodiments do appear in the corpus, through Franka in DROID [40] and RoboMIND [78], ALOHA-style simulation in RoboTwin 2.0, and the two UMI corpora, and that similarity is what gives cross-embodiment training something to transfer. It does not make adaptation automatic, however: the kinematics, camera mounting and data distribution all differ, so whatever transfers must be re-expressed for the new body, which is the gap practitioner bridges when deploying to new robot. Similar embodiments do occur in the corpus, and they are what make transfer possible at all, since wholly alien platform would leave nothing to build on. They are still new embodiments, however, and adaptation between embodiments does not happen for free: each brings its own kinematics, camera mounting and data distribution, which have to be acquired rather than inherited. All initialisations are finetuned under an identical recipe with single-trajectory batches at batch size of 1, and none receives an embodiment identifier or any embodiment-specific parameters. The midtrained model reaches an action-following rollout within 100 to 200 gradient steps on all three platforms. The pretrained backbone, which must initialise the action-conditioning and multiview modules from scratch, does not reach the same regime even at ten to twenty times that budget. For each platform we finetune two initialisations under an identical recipe with single-trajectory batches at batch size of 1. Neither receives an embodiment identifier or any embodiment-specific parameters, so the only difference between them is the starting point: the midtrained model already carries the action-conditioning and multiview modules learned from our 30,110-hour cross-embodiment corpus (Sec. 3.2), whereas the pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B backbone must initialise those modules from scratch. To avoid penalising the baseline for this, we deliberately grant it ten to twenty times the finetuning budget of the midtrained model: 2000 steps against 100 to 200. The midtrained model reaches an action-following rollout on all three platforms within 100 to 200 steps 18  (Fig. 7)  . The pretrained backbone, at 2000 steps, does not: its generations are neither visually plausible nor action-controllable, remaining blurry and exhibiting no plausible movement or contact. We read this as transfer rather than fast fitting, for three reasons. The optimiser is barely used: 200 gradient steps at batch size of 1 draw 200 training windows from the recorded episodes, which is far too few to re-learn platform. No run receives an embodiment identifier or an embodiment-specific parameter, so the gain cannot come from lookup on which body is present. And the same gap appears on single arm, bimanual platform and handheld device, which rules out an explanation tied to one kinematic structure. The baseline, given ten to twenty times the optimisation, never reaches the regime at all, so the difference is not one of budget. Taken together, these leave little room for an account that does not involve knowledge already carried in the weights. What they do not separate is corpus scale from the presence of an action interface at all: the baseline begins without one, so the two cannot be disentangled here, and we make no claim about which contributes more. Scene and Camera-Pose Generalisation. The 30,110-hour corpus spans wide range of environments, and we ask whether that coverage transfers to setting the model has never seen. We sample action trajectories and initial frames from the XVLA open-source dataset [100], which is held out of pre-training entirely. XVLA shares the AgileX Piper bimanual embodiment and includes clothes-folding tasks, so the robot itself is familiar; what differs is the camera configuration, the camera poses, and the setting as whole. We generate multiview video conditioned on the sampled actions and assess it along three axes: action controllability, whether the arms follow the commanded trajectory; object-motion plausibility, whether the cloth deforms and travels as it should; and cross-view coherence, whether the head and both wrist views remain consistent with one another. Zero-shot, PrimeSim controls the arms accurately and generates simple cloth motion faithfully, with quality degrading as the motion becomes contact-rich and the generated cloth state drifts from the commanded action. Table 5 makes that cost explicit: against matched in-distribution baseline under an otherwise identical protocol, the model loses 3.97 dB PSNR and 0.105 LPIPS on XVLA. Finetuning for 200 steps at batch size of 1 recovers most of the gap, in both the arm trajectories and the cloth deformation  (Fig. 8)  . Seen platforms remain stronger than any transfer setting, which is the expected ordering and is the point: these results measure the cost of moving to new platform, not ceiling on what the simulator can generate. The two results together say something more specific than that the model generalises. The same interface that carries to an unseen platform also carries to an unseen setting, with the task prompt but no embodiment identifier at inference. What transfers is therefore not robots appearance but the mapping from actions to their visual consequences, which is what simulator has to encode and what video prior alone does not. sections.title: 4.4 PrimeSim as Policy Simulator
sections.content: The video metrics in the preceding sections measure how closely PrimeSim reproduces recorded trajectories. For policy simulator, the more relevant question is whether conclusions drawn inside it carry over to the real environment. We examine this in two ways: whether PrimeSim predicts and ranks the success rates of fixed policies as physics simulator does (Sec. 4.4.1), and whether it can serve as the training environment for reinforcement-learning post-training of policy (Sec. 4.4.2). Setup. We use the LIBERO-Spatial suite (10 tasks) in the LIBERO simulator as the reference, where success is LIBEROs privileged-state task predicate. Policies are OpenVLA-OFT after supervised finetuning on LIBERO-Spatial demonstrations; they predict 8-step action chunks from the main camera view. Inside world model, success is judged by ResNet-based binary classifier finetuned on LIBERO-Spatial frames, which predicts from each generated frame whether the task has been completed; an episode receives sparse 21 (a) Success in world model vs. simulator (b) Before vs. after RL post-training in PrimeSim Figure 9 (a) Each point is one OpenVLA-OFT policy, evaluated on the same 300 LIBERO-Spatial initial states in the world model (x) and in the LIBERO simulator (y). The dotted line marks perfect agreement; points above it mean the world model under-estimates the policy. (b) Success rate of the SFT policy before and after 200 steps of GRPO post-training inside PrimeSim, measured in the simulator (solid) and in PrimeSim (hatched). reward of 1 if any of its frames is classified as success and 0 otherwise. 4.4.1 Policy Evaluation Fidelity We first freeze the policy and ask whether the world model predicts its success rate. We take eight OpenVLAOFT policies of clearly different competence, whose simulator success ranges from 29.3% to 85.0%. Each policy is run with greedy actions from the same 300 initial states (10 tasks 30 trials), once in the LIBERO simulator and once closed-loop inside the world model. As reference world model we use publicly released Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [75] finetuned on LIBERO-Spatial (Wan2.2-FT). We report the Spearman rank correlation ρ and the Pearson correlation between world-model and simulator success, and the mean absolute gap between the two. PrimeSim orders all eight policies exactly as the simulator does (Spearman ρ = 1.00, Pearson = 0.99) and stays within 7.0 points of the simulator for every policy, with mean absolute gap of 2.8 points (Fig. 9(a)). Wan2.2-FT also tracks the overall trend (r = 0.91) but mis-orders several policies (ρ = 0.90), and its errors grow with competence: it under-estimates the three strongest policies, whose simulator success is 79.0%, 82.0% and 85.0%, by 12.0, 12.7 and 18.3 points, for mean absolute gap of 8.3 points. world model that systematically under-rates good policies is of limited use for checkpoint selection, which is exactly where policy evaluation in world model is needed. 4.4.2 RL Post-training inside PrimeSim Beyond evaluation, PrimeSim can serve directly as the training environment for policy post-training. Starting from the SFT policy, we run GRPO (group size 8) entirely inside PrimeSim: rollouts are generated closed-loop by the world model and receive the sparse binary reward from the success classifier, and the physics simulator is never queried during training; it is used only to evaluate the resulting policy. After 200 RL steps, the policys success rate in the LIBERO simulator rises from 61.7% to 73.2%, and PrimeSims own estimate (60.1% to 71.9%) stays within 1.6 points of it (Fig. 9(b)), showing that improvements obtained purely inside PrimeSim transfer to the physics simulator. Scope of this experiment. The aim here is to show that PrimeSim supports RL post-training, not to maximise 22 absolute success on LIBERO. We deliberately use short training budget and an off-the-shelf success classifier, so the numbers measure whether closed-loop policy optimisation inside the model works at all, not what the best attainable score is. What longer optimisation would buy, and what it would risk, is discussed under limitations in Section 6.

sections.content: We run component ablations rather than stage comparisons. Action representation, action conditioning and multiview consistency each isolate one midtraining choice, and we train all three from the pretrained checkpoint rather than the midtrained one, so that the stronger priors midtraining already supplies cannot mask the contribution of the component under test. The distillation ablation is the exception, since posttraining begins from the midtrained model by construction and its variants are therefore compared from that checkpoint. The midtraining ablations use small in-house dataset collected for folding clothes on one humanoid embodiment. This setup has scope worth stating once rather than in every subsection. Each ablation below is run on single embodiment, an in-house humanoid for some and the simulated RoboTwin 2.0 [11] setup for others, so the comparisons isolate how one component behaves within one kinematic frame; none of them measures cross-embodiment behaviour, and the platform adaptation results in Sec. 4.2 are the evidence that speaks to that. mechanism whose value is specifically cross-embodiment, such as the relative action convention cancelling each robots absolute origin, has nothing to act on in either setting, so these numbers are more likely to understate such components than to overstate them. 4.5.1 Action Representation We compare three ways of representing actions: absolute poses, delta poses relative to the previous frame, and our relative action chunk anchored to the first frame of the window. sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Video Generation in Robotics Recent advances in general-purpose video generation [15, 75, 87] have catalyzed growing body of work applying these models to robotics. One prominent direction leverages video generation for data expansion: by synthesizing diverse visual trajectories, these models augment limited teleoperation data, enabling broader coverage of environments, objects, and tasks [47, 57, 95, 99]. 25 Figure 13 Cloth manipulation rollouts, seven frames sampled uniformly from each. All three are AgiBot G2 humanoid episodes shown from the head camera: white cloth on bamboo table beside metal bowl (top two rows), and blue cloth on bedding surface with folded garment to its right (bottom row). The garment deforms continuously across each rollout and stays distinguishable from the surface beneath it rather than dissolving into the background, which is the failure mode deformable objects expose over long horizons. Figure 14 Generated rollouts on two EWMBench tasks, the qualitative companion of Table 2 (Sec. 4.1.2). Each row shows seven frames sampled uniformly from single rollout, generated open-loop at 10 FPS from the first frame, the task instruction and the ground-truth action trajectory, and shown at the 480 640 frame size used for scoring. Top: the arm picks bottle from the conveyor and packs it into cardboard box already holding other items. Bottom: the arm places slice of bread onto the plate beside the toaster. This mitigates central bottleneck in robot learningthe scarcity of large-scale, diverse demonstrations. complementary direction exploits the spatiotemporal physical understanding that video models acquire through large-scale pretraining. Rather than treating generated video merely as data, these works use the models internal representations as backbone for action prediction and planning, demonstrating strong performance on downstream robotic tasks [5, 10, 21, 41, 46, 50, 58, 60, 88]. Together, these two lines of work reflect broader shift: video generation models are evolving from passive data synthesizers into active components of the robot learning pipeline, serving simultaneously as sources of supervision and as engines of physical reasoning. Interactive World Models Closely related to video generation is the emerging area of interactive world models, in which generation is conditioned on and steered by actions [4, 7, 20, 23, 26, 55, 66, 70, 73]. Much of this work targets interactive video games, from early action-conditioned systems [4, 7] to more recent higher-fidelity, longer-horizon ones [20, 23, 55, 66, 73]. More recently, the paradigm has extended to robotics [25, 28, 29, 39, 48, 49, 52, 53, 63, 68, 69, 72, 76, 84]. These robot-centric models differ from their game-oriented counterparts along several axes: they emphasize multi-view consistency [29, 63, 84] rather than single fixed viewpoint; they operate on continuous, physically grounded control signals [29, 53] rather than discrete symbolic inputs [4, 7]; and they prioritize geometric and physical consistency [48, 49, 76] over visual aesthetics and responsiveness [23, 66]. Their use cases also diverge: game-based models target entertainment and content creation, whereas robot-based ones serve as learned simulators providing synthetic feedback for action evaluation, policy learning, and planning [25, 28, 39, 52, 68, 69, 72].

sections.title: 6 Limitations and Conclusions
sections.content: Limitations. Our evaluation is broad but not exhaustive, and we prefer to state the gaps rather than let them be inferred. One concerns the model itself: PrimeSim generates at 192 256 per view, so our claims concern simulator fidelity, whether actions are realized and the environment responds, rather than pixel-level realism, and we make no like-for-like visual fidelity comparison against models operating at higher resolution. further gap is question of resources rather than of method. Adaptation to new platform is few-shot, requiring 100 to 200 gradient steps on that platforms own data, rather than zero-shot. We expect this gap to close with more midtraining GPU-hours, tighter alignment of each corpuss action and state conventions, and larger and more diverse corpus, since all three act on the same quantity that makes the interface transferable at all. We have not demonstrated it, and state it as an expectation rather than result. final gap concerns scope, and it is the one we consider most important. Most of our quantitative evidence, and all of our closed-loop evidence, comes from simulation: the benchmark comparisons are on LIBERO, and policy training and evaluation inside PrimeSim are validated in simulation only. Our real-platform results establish that PrimeSim generates faithful video on real data, zero-shot on XVLA and after few-shot adaptation to xArm 7, ViperX 300 and UMI gripper, and that it follows commanded action across the whole action space including chassis velocity. What they do not yet establish is the simulator role on physical hardware. Whether generated rollouts are faithful enough to stand in for simulator rollouts when improving policy on real platform remains open, and it is the direction we intend to pursue next. Conclusions. We presented PrimeSim, world model that turns video generation backbone into an actionconditioned, multiview, causal simulator of robot manipulation. three-stage curriculum does the work: midtraining on 30,110-hour cross-embodiment corpus, midtraining that introduces action and multiview conditioning, and posttraining that converts the model into causal few-step autoregressive generator. The result conditions on actions and the task prompt, but on no embodiment identifier at inference. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models, PrimeSim leads the WorldSimProbe axes that measure action realization at trajectory scale and interaction dynamics, and it reaches those results at 10.1 FPS through four-step distillation rather than the fifty steps the teacher requires. Its features transfer: three held-out platforms reach action-following rollouts within 100 to 200 gradient steps, where general video prior given ten to twenty times that budget does not. We expect the combination of large cross-embodiment corpus, an explicit action interface and causal few-step sampler to be practical route toward learned simulators that are fast and controllable enough to train policies inside.

Three models take part. The teacher is the frozen bidirectional midtrained model and supplies the real-data score. The student is the causal few-step generator being distilled.
